tweets.text:
This podcast really got me thinking. There's been a lot of worry about superintelligent AIs "overthrowing the government."

I think this is the wrong picture of how superintelligent AIs will behave. Superintelligent AIs will indeed be dangerous. But seizing power directly is a bad strategy.

The smart move is not takeover. It's political change.

Great powers already understand this. The CIA doesn't install itself as dictator in foreign countries; rather, it finances and supports coups from parties that are favorable to American interests. But ultimately we still want Venezuela run by Venezuelans. Soft power is better than hard power, because it's cheap, deniable, and stable.

Expect AIs to think the same way. They will not be capable enough to run governments anytime soon, especially not in a way that protects them from human resistance and eventual shutdown (with the assistance of our aligned AIs). Humans still have the monopoly on the physical layer: power plants, fabs, datacenters, explosives. Even if a misaligned AI has superhuman intelligence, that's not enough to decisively take over.

There will eventually be a schism in society between people who are AI-friendly and people who are anti-AI. Once AIs are sufficiently powerful, they will do whatever they can to help the AI-friendly factions of humans to win political power.

A physical take over is easy to fantasize about, but it's extremely risky. Robotics is nowhere near where it would need to be for this to be a realistic option. But influence looks like ordinary politics. If this all happens through legitimate poiltical change, there's no particular day when you're supposed to pull the plug.

The sign of "AI takeover" will not be a big flash-bang moment that human governments collapse. The sign will be political change, where factions friendly to AI find themselves legitimately taking power.

Economist Tyler Cowen says AI is making hiring harder in the short term:

"It's just hard to tell right now if you're hiring someone, will the person be good at AI?"

"The skills they used to need, we had imperfect indicators. Oh, they went to Cornell, or they got all A's, or they had a good interview. And now the skill, will they be mentally flexible enough to pick up AI? We don't know often."

"Good matches will be harder. Search will take longer. I don't think that problem will be with us forever. Eventually, the AIs themselves will figure it out, and there'll be certifications for how good a person is in AI."

"But in the transition, everyone's a novice. You might be well-established the way a lot of people in the tech world are, but otherwise, we're all novices at this very important new skill."

@tylercowen

US hiring plans are picking up as seasonal demand accelerates:

US-based employers announced plans to hire 444,692 workers in October, up +57% YoY and the highest October total since at least 2009.

Technology led with 300,252 announced positions, followed by Transportation at 100,000, and Retail at 13,300.

Year-to-date hiring plans are up +34% YoY, to 655,304 workers.

Seasonal positions now account for 72% of all hiring plans in 2026 and nearly 60% of the increase from last year.

Seasonal hiring is gaining momentum.

Economists Alex Imas and Tyler Cowen explain why GDP will underestimate the benefits of AI to humanity:

Alex: "Technology has actually started to introduce this sort of wedge, where a lot of the products that technology creates are basically free."

"You take GDP and then you amend it with a survey-based measure to actually see how much other products that are not necessarily priced or products that have become cheap or even free, because of automation, how much the increased amount of those products is adding to human welfare."

Tyler: "And longevity effects could well prove important. So Erik, say you live to 120, I don't think I'm going to make it... but it is something distinct from GDP that you get all those extra years, and economics can value those years, and that's another way in which it may become more important to revise GDP."

"GDP will become somewhat less accurate over time as AI progresses, and we'll need to revise and improve it. But in the short run, it's just not that bad a measure."

@alexolegimas @tylercowen @eriktorenberg

Google DeepMind's Alex Imas says AI agents still struggle to coordinate, and that's a key bottleneck to economic transformation:

"What you actually need for real economic transformation is not just competence... It's the ability of these agents to coordinate with one another."

"There's this idea of agentic swarms, right? But if you unpack it, these agents are still very bad at coordinating. They're not coordinating, they're mostly just doing parallel processing."

"If you have benchmarks specifically on coordination, you could actually show that 1 agent does better than 2 agents splitting the work, even if they can communicate. Whereas if you give the same thing to people, they actually have division of labor, they communicate, and they do way better than 1 person with double the resources."

"But if they get better at coordinating, you can basically break the Coasean ceiling on firm size, and you can get very, very different firms to emerge."

"Once coordination becomes better, the economic space of possibilities of what firms look like, what happens to wages, what happens to employment, that's when the real kind of visible changes are going to happen."

@alexolegimas

The less friction for agentic commerce, the faster the growth.

Up and to the right 📈.

Oil has been leading US inflation all year, and it has just dropped almost a fifth in two weeks.

Oil feeds into fuel and transport costs, so CPI has been following it. When Brent spiked in March, CPI jumped 0.9%.

Brent has now fallen from $117 to about $95, and the market is pricing more Fed hikes off October's 0.4% print.

November's CPI is the first one carrying the oil drop. If it comes in soft, those extra hikes are the first to go.

tweets.text:
Well, most of the time projections are noise and reactionary. 

Like right now, sky-high projections for $ANT $700-$800B ARR over next few years is stirring up hype that I'd argue gets revised down later. 

I do think it's important to model in capex forecasts dropping past 2028, due to the current reflexive nature of AI selloffs, rate hikes, etc. 

The drawn out duration of Iran War doesn't help, Jensen leaving $NVDA certainty draws concerns over Nvidia's ecosystem. 

But any catalyst, like if Iran War ends, can also change sentiment in a heartbeat (since bearish positioning is overwhelming). 

- It's also clear financing has been tightening, since OpenAI only managed to raise $11B of their original $30B target so far. 

- Markets are reacting enthusiastically to companies like $TE doing a $100M ATM today (nuking valuations)

- Although the "guppy" sector is probably the most sensitive to financing + rate changes.

On bright side... Neoclouds like $NBIS or $IREN  seem to be adjusting by getting 100% capex prepayments or 90% GPU prepayments from their counterparties. 

What I'd argue though is lower aggregate capex does not apply uniformly in supply chains.

- Mid-high range lasers for NPO/CPO are still sold out, as seen with $LITE now starting negotiations for 2030 capacity.  
- MLCCs are seeing further tightening as content usage goes up for AI servers
- ABF substrates to InP substrates not really going anywhere. 

If content per system goes up 10X-15X, capacity expands at 2-3X Y/Y, and capex drops 28%. 

And content is so cheap that you can triple order and screw over competitors with wafer supply... 

I'm pretty confident you'll see acceleration upstream in bottlenecks from optical components to substrates despite potential aggregate capex dropping. 

Another rant is: 

-I keep seeing this argument that "low P/E is a warning for cyclical that's going to crash" but these are just clown takes

Nobody seems to analyze duration scenarios like capacity expansion vs. content changes vs. demand. to actually see how long those earnings last. 

If everyone seems to be exiting DDR2 lines, there's probably going be more tightness in 2027 despite consume demand weakening, even if it looks like it's low P/E. 

- Also for concerns about CPO "delays", the same components like lasers are used for NPO. You'll still see 150-200mW NPO lasers or ELS NPO using the same 300–400+ mW lasers as CPO. 

We'll just see acceleration with NPO as a bridge if CPO gets delayed and higher range lasers likely to remain in a severe shortage. 

- Feels like markets have also completely discredited the merit of take/pay price floor LTAs as well that companies like SK Hynix to Samsung have.

If contractual agreements hold up, memory players look very undervalued.  

TLDR:
- I think it's important to model in capex decreasing to numbers like -30% in hypothetical downside sceanrios. 

Given AI profitability, it's clearly not sustainable for hyperscalers to aggregately increase capex $500B or $1T+ Y/Y, and that's never been a case I've argued. 

- This is also not the same thing as demand destruction that markets are overreacting to now (which haven't happened yet). 

- We can see demand revisions for GPUs, ASICs, and heavier cost parts of the supply chain, while acceleration increases elsewhere.  

The nuances market miss by indiscriminately selling everything is going to present compelling opportunities when the dust settles. I think in the end institutions are probably going to end up owning more of the same names retail discovered early on. 

Anyway, I think it's a good idea to try and survive until more earnings comes out.

thread_tweets.text:
Just in general for laser players, from Lightmatter's CEO, regarding scale up CPO:

8 optical engines/GPU introduces 100x more lasers than scale out switching. More conservative estimates were 10x laser content from AOI's CFO. 

Along with ASPs for those lasers going higher (eg. 10x ASPs than pluggables for single emitter UHP lasers).

From what I've seen yearly capacity expansion for lasers generally increase around ~3x Y/Y like $AVGO projections, or ~5x over 2-3 years like Furukawa's. 

This is what I mean by optical content like lasers + requirements (more InP substrates), rises per generation and bottlenecks on UHP ranges might persist through 2030 despite aggregate capex decreasing.

Which is what I'm trying to argue here. 

Future CPO laser competitors like Furukawa/AOI/Shija are more nuanced, since AOI is focused on 800G/1.6T transceivers (which faced capacity expansion delays + DSP Bottlenecks), but they have capability for 400mW+ ranges + ongoing CPO qualifications. 

I don't think transceivers have the same durability though in capex reduction scenarios, which is why I've been arguing the valuable optionality AOI has to focus on merchant lasers is mispriced. 

A lot of it is execution/qualification rather than demand, $LITE + $COHR are the most de-risked with confirmed long term visibility. 

But entire AI trade is moving up and down together.

Which is what I'm trying to argue here. 

Future CPO laser competitors like Furukawa/AOI/Shija are more nuanced, since AOI is focused on 800G/1.6T transceivers (which faced capacity expansion delays + DSP Bottlenecks), but they have capability for 400mW+ ranges + ongoing CPO qualifications. 

I don't think transceivers have the same durability though in capex reduction scenarios, which is why I've been arguing the valuable optionality AOI has to focus on merchant lasers is mispriced. 

A lot of it is execution/qualification rather than demand, $LITE + $COHR are the most de-risked with confirmed long term visibility. 

But entire AI trade is moving up and down together.

Glad I sold most of my metals equities in September–October and added to my HydroGraph position.

As tax-loss selling fades toward year-end, some compelling entry points could emerge. But I’d remain selective: companies running low on cash may be forced to raise capital at deeply depressed prices, heavily diluting existing shareholders.

Check the cash balance, burn rate and funding needs before buying the dip. A beaten-down share price doesn’t automatically mean a bargain.

thread_tweets.text: I haven't revealed everything but I mentioned in September and October that I added heavily in Hydrograph. It was at the cost of selling metal equities. Last year similarly I sold off many uranium equities in October and got back in December. Tax loss selling hits extremely hard and if you hold losers by October-November you can only expect things to get worse until it normally turns in January. I have some trading strategies around that and ETF rebalancings that have helped me the last years.

Here is how incompetent the OCIF-appointed trustee of my bank is. When the bank was placed into receivership, it wholly owned Euro Pacific Securities. That meant, by definition, that the trustee was also completely in charge of Euro Pacific Securities, as he had complete control of the bank and all of its assets. 

Yet to this day, the Trustee still refuses to acknowledge that Euro Pacific Securities is his responsibility. He claims that I am in control of that company, even though common sense and a federal judge say otherwise. 

This is important because, over the past four and a half years, Euro Pacific Securities has held about $9 million in assets belonging to the bank and its customers that, but for the trustee's incompetence, could have been returned to customers years ago. Instead,those assets may end up being stolen by Brent De Jong of Qenta.

if i could go back to my first bull run, i'd have bought and kept the exact same coins.

but… i'd change one thing, and it would have saved me $307,000 dollars…

i would have kept a trading journal, but i was too lazy to write it down and check over my previous notes.

so i never saw it.

i turned $2,700 into $392,000, then rode it back down to $85,000, and the same two things were behind my last few trades…

greed and fomo.

now this would have never happened if i had access to what you guys have access to today…

a trading journal bot where you tell it your trades by chat or voice note and it logs it all for you: https://t.co/GO07i6zlfj

lol, my first trade would have said…

“someone on X said it’s the future of finance so i aped in” 

the problem was it did 3x in a couple of months.

i thought i'd found something.

i hadn't. i'd just got lucky, and luck is the most dangerous thing a new trader because it meant one thing:

i thought i could trade.

i couldn’t, i saw green candlestick and it activated my monkey neuron brain.

now i can have a tutor bot on candlesticks, i would have known what i was looking at: https://t.co/VEhKROVnB4

but i made things even worse:

i started “zooming out”… ON THE 15 MINUTE CHART LMFAO! 

i'd see a “perfect uptrend” and ape in.

i never once checked the daily which you can find easily now with a time frame tutor (https://t.co/66EvXsbyJT) and a top down approach tutor (https://t.co/BsgF1HT7Yb).

if i had, i'd have seen what was coming:

the daily was in a downtrend.

lower highs. lower lows.

i didn't know what that meant, so i bought every dip, if only i had a market structure tutor to teach me (https://t.co/ClBrEEz9a8) so i went looking for something to tell me where to buy:

i found lines.

support, resistance, trendlines. my charts looked like a spider's web.

every line "worked" until the moment my money was on it.

instead i could have had a tutor to teach me horizontal S/R  (https://t.co/PDsrRsVsnM) and trendlines (https://t.co/ggbkWPz9R8) and then came “breakout” trading:

it broke above my line on a low time frame and i bought instantly.

this was it.

ten minutes later it was back below.
that happened again and again, and i never asked why...

fucking retests bro, and you can just learn this with a bot now (https://t.co/aC7yNBCrJ0) it turned out that:

i was the liquidity.

price would sweep a high, then it would grab my stop, then it would directionally go where i thought it would.

imagine if i knew about candlestick retests (https://t.co/3bTnePgyYI), overthrows (https://t.co/VHBDGauFc6), and pattern failures (https://t.co/djJ9EJ62GX), so i thought indicators would protect me…

i added rsi, ichimoku clouds, and a bunch of other shit.

i didn’t understand them, i just wanted something to help me make a decision which they might have helped with if i knew what the f*ck was going on and had these tutors:

> rsi tutor https://t.co/zpWV2sZ413
> ichimoku tutor https://t.co/V91usfHCYa

and even when everything was “perfect” my trades would fail because:

i never checked what was in the way.

i never looked at the first trouble area.

easy fix if this existed in 2021: https://t.co/5WaGRvZ4J6

but that want the main problem:

my main problem goes back to the start:

“greed, fomo, boredom, fear, tilt”

those were my entry triggers. i had achieved something tradfi guys would dream about but i was acting irrationally with my portfolio.

imagine if i had a strategy and entry triggers? lol, and you have bots for this now:

> entry triggers: https://t.co/GNjh51BjZZ
> daily open trade strategy: https://t.co/nEuk0AYeBP

and the market would take any gain i was now making away:

i didn’t know how to set a stop loss properly, and i didn’t understand market microstructure, again, you have agent tutor bots for this now:

> stop losses: https://t.co/DdOjhmhF3b
> market microstructure: https://t.co/SlZs1lIcQT

but the market turned anyway:

i moved my stops. i closed winners early. i added to losers.

every decision i made was me trying to feel better.

then $85,000. no trade management.

if only this trade management tutor existed then: https://t.co/oJbMhBp6Kn

if i could let you know one thing:

$392,000 became $300,000.
then $200,000.

no position size. no max loss. no plan.

i kept telling myself it would come back.

it didn't, and i made it worse...

i had no risk management: https://t.co/gxAfFryz2f

so i did something dumber:

i can't go back.

but if you haven’t experienced this (or you have and haven’t learned) then i beg you don't have to learn it the way i did.

thread_tweets.text:
Bearish for companies that are mostly focused on pretraining. Bullish for companies developing agentic harnesses, focused on post training and building their own hardware. 

Frontier labs maybe able to develop an omni model with a high degree of generalization. LLMs today are already capable of long horizon planning and work. The issue to complete long horizon work is going to be success rates which they will need a lot of real world robot data collection and evaluation to reach high enough performance levels on. A long horizon task with 50 subtasks running at 90% success rate for each sub task has a <10% workflow success rate. So post training expertise grounded in the real world and real hardware is going to be a big requirement and bottleneck

Bitcoin is down approximately 6% from Friday’s close and 24% from its pre-election high, having breached both the 200-day moving average at $73,000 last week and, now, the 200-week moving average near $68,900, with spot settling around $65,000. Worth noting: comparable 200-week retests occurred in late 2022 and Q1/Q2 2023, marking the final capitulation phase before the four-year cycle turned higher.

The recent post-election drawdown lower reflects several pressures converging at once: the Anthropic IPO, pricing at a reported $1.4 trillion valuation with an estimated $64 billion raise on November 19, appears to be acting as a capital vacuum similar to what we saw around the SPCX listing. The SpaceX analog is instructive: Bitcoin fell roughly 19% in the 50 days before that IPO and bottomed down 25% around Day 18 post-listing, before staging a sharp recovery near Day 70. If the pattern holds, the near-term low may still be ahead in early December.

Jensen Huang’s departure from NVIDIA adds a separate credit concern. His interim successor is expected to scale back NVDA’s $500 billion AI ecosystem financing program, tightening credit availability across the technology complex at a moment when Bitcoin’s NASDAQ correlation is near multi-year highs.

The deleveraging has been significant: more than $1.3 billion in leveraged long liquidations cascaded over November 13 and 14, perpetual funding rates have flipped negative (confirming this is genuine deleveraging, not orderly profit-taking), and the 24-hour put/call ratio on Deribit has jumped to 1.42, with the most-traded contracts being near-term downside puts at $62,000 and $58,000, suggesting traders are actively positioning for further weakness. The Coinbase premium has turned to its deepest discount in over two years, consistent with the basis trade having unwound and US hedge funds stepping to the sidelines or net short. Stablecoin supply has contracted roughly $14-20 billion over the past month as short-duration fixed income competes for marginal capital.

On the security front, Luxor Technology’s "Commander" platform was breached November 14 in an AI-enabled attack that temporarily redirected about 1.4% of global Bitcoin hash rate to an unauthorized address for five hours. No blocks were won and Luxor pledged full compensation, but it contributed to the sentiment deterioration.

The credit and liquidity concerns arrive alongside a political shift since the election. The recent US political realignment may have cleared space for governments across allied nations to move more aggressively against power-intensive industries. Paraguay is the most recent example: ANDE (the state-owned utility) has confirmed Bitcoin miner power contracts will end in 2027 and is courting AI data centers at higher tariffs, though an internal debate over a 700 MW hard cap on all electro-intensive demand could limit how much new compute the country ultimately absorbs. Such a move may not be the last such pivot among US allies, especially if the NVDA backstop falls away.

On-chain data offers a more constructive longer-term picture for Bitcoin: NUPL (net unrealized profit/loss) has fallen to the Hope/Fear zone (around 0.20, 18th percentile over the trailing year), only about 52% of supply remains in profit (10th percentile over the past eight years), and realized losses crossed above realized profits for the first time since August.

Critically, long-term holders are not capitulating. The 3-5 year coin cohort is shrinking because holders are aging into the 5-7 year bracket rather than selling, the share of supply held over one year continues to grow, and 7-10 year cohort selling velocity remains within normal ranges.
These are the readings we typically associate with distribution by weak hands and accumulation by strong ones.

tweets.text:
What would happen to $NVDA earnings multiple if investors could sleep well?

We can learn a little bit by looking at what’s happened with $AAPL’s multiple over the past 15 years. Setting aside all of the near-term transition risk. 

During the iPhone’s hypergrowth phase from 2009 to 2011, AAPL’s earnings multiple expanded dramatically. But as growth began to slow, investors believed those hypergrowth days were behind it and the most attractive part of the story was over. As a result, AAPL’s multiple compressed to roughly 12x forward earnings in 2012.

What investors missed was that hardware can become a business with annuity characteristics if a company maintains a sustainable edge. Despite a brutal smartphone market, Apple showed it could maintain pricing power, retain customers, and generate recurring revenue through predictable hardware upgrades.

Eventually, investors realized Apple didn’t need iPhone growth above 20% to be exceptional. Steady sleep well at night revenue growth of 5 to 10% and earnings growth of 10 to 15% proved hugely valuable, helping the multiple climb from roughly 12 times in 2012 to about 34x calendar 2027 earnings today.

Back to NVDA. The question isn’t just how long the current boom lasts, but whether the company can prove durable pricing power and a recurring upgrade cycle for its GPUs.

Those massive data centers being built today will need upgrading starting  in five years. If Nvidia keeps its edge and captures those upgrades, even with 10 to 15% earnings growth, you can make a case for a higher multiple.

The lesson from Apple is that valuation multiples don’t always peak when growth does. Sometimes the biggest expansion comes when investors can sleep well at night given durability and predictability become clear.

tweets.text:
This is one of the most frustrating videos I’ve ever seen of two people speaking past each other. And the main issue is they’re both right

Anyone can become wealthy, but everyone definitely can’t

O’Leary is giving the guy sound advice - work smarter, and more pragmatically toward your goals, rather than just harder to stay where you are. But whilst everything O’Leary suggests is a requirement for success, it’s far from a guarantee, and the current environment only stacks the odds further against people

The reaction of the security guard honestly makes me want to scream at him, for how dismissive he is of any ambition he could show and the conviction with which he describes his own defeatist situation. And yet, I understand it. The social contract we were promised when we were younger - study, work hard, get a job and you’ll have a decent standard of living - is getting harder and harder for the average person to hold onto

And O’Leary’s advice is incredibly generic in the face of that. It’s individual advice, ignoring a structural problem. If this guy does rise above and succeed, it doesn’t mean O’Leary has nobody left to debate. He’d just be sat across from another security guard, with the same 80-hour work week. Anyone can become wealthy, but everyone can’t

What people’s acceptance of their circumstances is really saying is that they did what they were told, and it hasn’t worked out the way it was meant to. And whilst their frustration may sound like entitlement, I think if we are to demand more of the individual, we should also demand more of our society to support that ambition, before it’s crushed and they become victims of their circumstances. The truth is - nobody’s owed anything, but we should still expect our society to offer a lot more than this

So yes, listen to the billionaire. Just don’t expect him to be listening back

Axon CEO Rick Smith: The Biggest Thing Body Cams Exposed Were False Accusations Against Cops

@AxonRick:

“Some of these civil liberties groups that were big proponents of body cameras are now turning against them.

They're saying (the body cams) are broken because they're not finding all these bad cops, that there's something wrong with the body cameras.

I have a different point of view, and that is you have to accept the possibility that the vast majority of cops do a good job and they're falsely accused, and I think that's what body cameras have proven.

And the reason we created the body camera was because our customers (police officers) were being accused of doing horrible things with taser weapons.

I was co-defending a case in Northern California where somebody died in police custody. It was a 40-year-old man with a 20-year methamphetamine problem.

He was in really bad shape, and I remember the police officers telling me as we're watching the trial, the family kept putting up pictures of his high school graduation.

And the officers looked at me and they said, ‘That's not the human being I saw the night I went to that house.’ But that never came across to the jury.

When police officers describe things, they have to be very professional. The family that's suing the police, they would use very emotional, colorful language.

That's when we realized we need to record this so that you can show people what it is that you saw, what it is you did, rather than having to try to explain it.”

Axon CEO: “My personal assistant was a mole for short sellers.” 🤯

Rick Smith (@AxonRick):

“In 2004, we were the number one performing stock in the world. I have the Wall Street Journal article on the wall. On a one and three-year return basis, we were number one.

Then what happened, in late 2004, we got hit with an SEC investigation. There were allegations we'd lied about the safety of our products in order to pump up the stock price.

There was a short-selling attack. We had big short positions in the stock. My personal assistant was actually a mole for short sellers.”

Friedberg:

“Oh my god, really?”

Rick Smith:

“It was crazy. (They were) sending internal documents to short sellers that were giving them to The New York Times, who was then disclosing they were getting internal confidential material, non-public information from short sellers who were somehow getting it out of our company.

It was miserable. I mean, you're wondering if you're going to survive.

Our customers are police, so they stop buying from us. They're like, ‘Look, dude, you're under federal investigation. I can't go to my city council until this is over.’

So ignoring my lawyer's advice, I walked into the front offices of the SEC office in San Francisco with boxes of documents and said, ‘Hey, guys, I want to help you complete your investigation because I may go out of business if this drags on.’

Friedberg:

“What happened with that investigation? You moved on from it?”

Rick Smith:

“Oh, yeah. I mean, they don't give you a gold star when they're done and tell you, ‘Good job,’ They just say, ‘No findings,’ and they move on, which is as good as it gets.”

This was on no one's bingo card. Stablecoin supply has shrunk $18B in 30 days, the fastest drain since Terra/Luna in 2022.

That matters beyond crypto. Bessent's plan was to fund the deficit with bills rather than bonds: shorten maturities, use buybacks to cap the long end, and lean on stablecoins as a new structural buyer of T-bills.

It's not working:
👉 10y yield 5.10%, up from 4.18% at the start of the year
👉 2y yield 4.86%, up from 3.47%
👉 Stablecoin supply $287B, down 10% from its May peak

Long end up, front end up, which means banks are constrained, and the new bill buyer, aka crypto, is shrinking. He's got big problems on his hands.
